With the English top-flight a state of flux right now, it's not hard to yearn for years gone by.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the so-called “Best League in the World™”, it’s safe to say the Premier League is currently experiencing a full-blown existential crisis.

The bombshell announcement of Manchester City’s guilt on all but one of their 115 charges has left the game feeling more hollow than ever before. Is there a title race? Who’s going down? What is real? Does any of this mean anything? Throw in the continued abomination that is VAR and more, and it’s all just a bit bleak.

So with that, let’s cast our minds to a simpler, purer time, the much-fabled “Barclays era” of 2004 to 2016.

While football didn’t start in 1992, the Premier League did and by the early-to-mid 2000s, it was reaching its apex as the blood and thunder of decades prior fused with the new-found flair and panache to create a near-perfect concoction.

The current state of the English top-flight can be traced all the way back to the summer of 2003 with Roman Abramovich’s purchase of Chelsea. It was the moment the horse bolted and nothing has been the same since.

However, at the time, it was all just a little bit exciting and things really picked up 12 months later when Jose Mourinho landed in West London, rightly claiming to be the “Special One”. The reigning European Cup winner was joined by Rafael Benitez, who came to Liverpool after incredible success with Valencia.

Suddenly, Sir Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger were no longer the only gunslingers in town. The “Big Two” quickly became the “Big Four” as Mourinho romped to the league title - breaking numerous records - and Benitez amazingly won the Champions League. Istanbul and all that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The two Iberians changed so much in the English game. From how to set up a side to how to win the title - 4-4-2 and peaking after Christmas being swapped out for 4-3-3 and rapid-fast starts.

Liverpool’s fifth European Cup was significant for numerous reasons. It was their first in 21 years but also the first final featuring an English side in the 21st century. They had beaten Chelsea to get there, starting both an incredible rivalry between the clubs and managers, and a golden age for the Premier League.

Over the next four years, all of the then-”Big Four” made finals and there were three semi-finalists in every season from 06/07 to 08/09. The peak came in 2008 when each was knocked out by another with United eventually toppling Chelsea in the first all-English final in Moscow. In one of the odder paradoxes, England failed to qualify for the European Championships that summer.

Fergie’s empire had struck back with Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney at the forefront of it. In an era of elite pairings, there was no finer. Ronaldo’s Ballon d’Or win confirmed his status as the best player in the world, and the Premier League as truly the best league.

It was also a time of far less financial disparity with the rest of Europe, Milan and Inter lifting the Champions League in 2007 and 2010 respectively. Things would soon change and not for the better.

While the big boys competed for the biggest trophies, there were plenty of brilliant stories elsewhere. Harry Redknapp’s Portsmouth won the FA Cup in 2008, setting the tone for Wigan five years later in epic fashion against City months on from Swansea claiming the League Cup. Only Crystal Palace's success in 2025 has been comparable since.

Throw in Big Sam’s Bolton, Blackburn, Stoke, Hull and others and it was the last definitive age of the cult teams and cult heroes, or as they’ve become better known - The Barclaysmen. With the overload of data nowadays, another Michu-like madness feels further away than ever.

Abu Dhabi’s takeover of City in 2008 is the obvious place to pinpoint the beginning of the end, but Mourinho’s first Chelsea exit a year prior and Ronaldo’s first from United a year after moved the centre of attention from England to Spain.

While European success faded - a fate-like Chelsea were the only winners from 2008 to 2019 - there were still memorable domestic moments, two of which unfortunately led to City winning their first pair of Premier League titles. Agueroooooo and Gerrard’s slip may be rendered utterly irrelevant soon but the memories won’t. It was peak Premier League.

As was Sir Alex Ferguson’s last dance in 2013 and Leicester’s miracle title win in 2016, which will never be topped as the greatest achievement in the history of English football. That it came either side of Chelsea’s crooked titles and prior to City’s dodgy dominance makes it all the more appropriate as the ending of the last great era. And that goes for both in football and the world itself.

While the on-field action of the last decade may feel fraudulent, how we now consume football is also a far cry from those halcyon Barclays days.

Streaming was not yet a thing in 2004. Sky Sports was in its pomp. Super Sunday actually lived up to its billing as appointment viewing.

Influencers and content creators had not yet taken over. Gary Neville went past his winger on the overlap rather than host it. Social media was still fun for the most part.

We had Soccer AM and Goals on Sunday, Gillette Soccer Saturday and Match of the Day at elite levels, and even room for shows like Wayne Rooney’s Street Striker and Football’s Next Star.

Nostalgia is a helluva drug, but as Independent Panels decide the fate of English football past, present and future, it’s near-impossible to dispute that, like so much of entertainment, we had it so much better before.

One day, the pendulum will hopefully swing back in our favour but, for now, a rewatch of Premier League Years on Sky may be in order.

Peter writes freelance for FourFourTwo and has previous experience at Evening Standard and Football365 among several others. He now works for us alongside OneFootball, the Sporting News and Stats Perform. One of the very few Irish people living in London and even fewer to support Manchester United, he spends time away from football rewatching TV shows and attempting to play tennis.

#991. Mauricio Pochettino sends message to Man Utd fans ahead of first day: ‘Give me time’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino has arrived at Carrington after signing off his reign with the USA by beating Haiti on Tuesday night

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino said to “give him time” to make Manchester United the city’s dominant club again after taking charge of his last match in charge of the United States.

The US beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati to wrap up an 8-0 aggregate victory in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final.

AC Milan forward Christian Pulisic opened the scoring with a spectacular overhead kick and teenager Julian Hall doubled the hosts’ lead before half-time.

Pochettino will take charge of Manchester United for the first time against Liverpool on Sunday after being appointed to succeed Michael Carrick, and arrived at the club’s Carrington training ground on Wednesday afternoon as he began work as their new head coach.

Pochettino, who has signed a deal until the summer of 2029, jetted into Manchester after the victory over Haiti and was whisked to the club’s training base to meet United staff and start preparations his first match.

His final message as USA manager was towards United fans, asking for patients as he looked to restore the footballing hierarchy in Manchester to what it used to be.

Told by former Manchester City loanee DaMarcus Beasley that “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue” in the TNT Sports studio after the game, Pochettino responded: “You will see. Give me time.

“The new challenge is a big challenge, but at the same time it’s adrenalin you want to feel.

“We need to add our common sense… we know the situation is not a situation that deserves to be a club like Manchester United, the fan base is amazing.”

Pochettino heads to Old Trafford having led the US to the last 16 at this year’s World Cup on home soil.

“The mentality is to learn from everyone,” Pochettino told reporters. “You need to have an open mind because I think the players can teach us everyday, we are much better coaching staff now.

“Football is about attitude, and it’s about the approach. It’s about connection, feelings and communication.”

#990. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

DW has found that three-quarters of Russia's weightlifting team had no independent out-of-competition testing before this year's world championships, despite the country's doping history.

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."

WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

#988. Has Uefa fumbled the chance to bring down Gianni Infantino as Fifa president?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Infantino was badly wounded after his disastrous attempt to sell of stakes in the World Cup and Club World Cup. But ahead of Fifa’s presidential election, his strength appears restored

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It has been nearly four months since journalists at The Times and Financial Times exposed Gianni Infantino’s shady plan to sell off 20 per cent of the World Cup and other Fifa tournaments to private investors, having sought approval from JP Morgan Chase, Donald Trump’s son-in-law’s brother, but almost no one inside Fifa and absolutely no one in the wider football world.

It sparked a humiliating chain of events for Infantino. His senior advisor resigned calling it “a bad deal for football”. His chief operating officer said Fifa colleagues had been “deceived”. Uefa threatened to boycott future World Cups unless the scheme was scrapped. National associations withdrew their support and continental federations united against him. Fifpro, the global players’ union, accused Infantino of a “profound abuse of power”.

The scathing attacks kept coming and in that moment it seemed hard to imagine how Infantino could possibly struggle on, let alone stand in spring’s presidential election.

Yet ahead of Wednesday’s deadline for election rivals to submit their candidacy, Infantino’s strength appears largely restored. He sacked his most vocal critic inside Fifa, COO Kevin Lamour. He went on a round-the-world tour visiting more than 30 countries in an effort to shore up support. He vowed to vastly increase per-nation spending from $1m to $25m by January, enough to convince the president of the Asian confederation, Sheikh Salman Al-Khalifa, to U-turn and throw his weight behind Infantino’s re-election.

In the background, Uefa has been scrabbling around for a rival candidate. Aleksander Ceferin decided to stay on as Uefa president rather than risk taking on Infantino and losing. Arsene Wenger, Fifa’s head of football development, weighed up a bid but decided against it. So, with about 48 hours to go, Uefa revealed their candidate to challenge Infantino was a Frenchman named [checks notes] Philippe Diallo.

What do we know about Diallo? He is a trained lawyer, career sports administrator and the current head of the French Football Federation. His father was a Senegalese boxer and there is hope inside Uefa that African roots might help sway a few votes. But in a game of personalities, he is a worryingly low-profile figure. This is a man whose entire Wikipedia entry contains fewer words than the section of Infantino’s page labelled ‘honours and awards’, where you will find a series of titles about as meaningful as the Fifa Peace Prize, including a Friendship Medal from Vladimir Putin.

There is still time for sentiments to change, but right now Infantino is the clear frontrunner. He needs 106 votes of the 211 national associations, and is thought to hold large swathes of support throughout Africa (54 votes), Asia (47) and South America (10). He may even retain support in quiet corners of Europe too. Uefa’s disorganised attempts to line up an eye-catching contender have only bolstered Infantino’s position.

There is some disappointment within Uefa that Wenger didn’t step forward, though in reality he has always been an Infantino loyalist. Wenger’s condemnation of the World Cup sell-off was alarmingly slow and indirect, and he has shown little appetite to bite the hand that feeds him.

There remains some confidence of overcoming Infantino among figures inside Uefa, although much of it stems not from their election hopes but across the Atlantic, where another election may have changed the picture. The Democrats’ success in the recent US mid-terms will bolster their numbers in the House of Representatives from January, and they could then issue subpoenas to lay bare Infantino’s relationship with Trump.

There is also Uefa’s concerted pursuit of documents which it hopes will reveal the gory details of the sell-off plan. A New York court rejected Fifa’s attempts to block the documents from being released, although they are still yet to emerge. Uefa hopes they may lead to a criminal trial.

Infantino’s opponents within Uefa feel one of these avenues could lead to his downfall. It will have to be seismic: there is already plenty to criticise about his reign as Fifa president, and almost nothing has so far eroded his power.

Infantino performatively began his presidency on an Easyjet flight, yet he quickly got a taste for the good life and nobody seems to mind that he now flies around in private jets. There was the absurdity of Trump’s peace prize, and the brazen sporting scandal that was Folarin Balogun’s lifted suspension. Yet, ultimately, Infantino has been very good at delivering promised money for federations, and that happens to be a useful vote-returning mechanism.

Infantino shouldn’t really be standing in this election, of course. Fifa presidents are only supposed to serve a maximum of three four-year terms, but he found a loophole and Fifa “clarified” just before the Qatar World Cup that his first three years didn’t count, rather he was finishing Sepp Blatter’s work. He could now lead until 2031, completing a 15-year reign, quite the stint for a man who declared in his very first speech: “The new Fifa is a democracy, not a dictatorship.”

If the legal routes fail to remove Infantino, he could still be voted out when the presidential election comes around in March. But it seems only one man will stand to challenge him. And if you’ve got to the end of this article and forgotten his name, then that is part the problem.

The Brazilian forward struggled to find his best form at the Emirates Stadium, and he feels he was simply in the wrong place at the wrong time

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Timing is everything in football - and that goes for getting transfer moves right, too.

After seven years at Chelsea, Willian made the move across London to join Arsenal in 2020, which seemed like it should be a decent enough fit for all concerned.

But Willian has made no secret of the fact that he did not enjoy his time at the Emirates Stadium - and in hindsight, he believes he may simply have been the wrong player in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Willian told FourFourTwo: "These things happen in football. I had some personal frustrations and I couldn't perform on the pitch the way I had been performing at Chelsea.

"Arsenal were also a club that was changing a lot at that time. There were a lot of people leaving and a lot of new people coming in.

"It was a restructuring and I got caught up in the middle of it - and it's not easy.

I left a well-established club, winning almost every year, fighting for titles every year, and I joined a club that was trying to find a way to win titles again.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"So I got caught up in that situation, and that's why things didn't work out. It wasn't easy, but I really wasn't happy.

"The contract I had was actually a very big one, but it got to the point that money wasn’t enough.

"The most important thing is to be happy, to play with joy. I wasn't able to do so there, so I ended up asking to leave the club, leaving that contract behind."

After spending a year back in Brazil with Corinthians, Willian found a new home at Fulham in 2022 - and he credits Marco Silva with helping him to rediscover his spark.

He said: "When I left Brazil, my goal was to go to England, stay there, because I love the place and my agent lives there too.

"Therefore, I decided to be in London, have some meetings and see what the possibilities are. My agent said, ‘Marco Silva wants to talk to you’. We had a meeting with him, and he invited me to join training and see how I felt.

"It wasn't a trial, it was more to see if I could readjust, especially after what had happened to me at Arsenal.

"I really liked Marco’s style. I felt celebrated, and it's not flattery, but I felt that respect, that affection from everyone. I was very happy there at Fulham."

#986. What does Arteta do with Konsa once Saliba returns?

Ezri Konsa has starred for Arsenal at centre-back following his £55m move from Aston Villa this summer, but William Saliba has now returned to take back his position in the Arsenal team; the Gunners have important games against Man City, Real Madrid and Spurs after the break

Football Journalist @SamBIitz

Arsenal have a big set of fixtures coming up after the November international break. Big games require big team selections - and Mikel Arteta has a huge decision to make in his defence.

William Saliba is coming back, which is a major boost for the Premier League champions, but to say Arsenal have missed him in recent weeks has been an understatement. Ezri Konsa has stepped up.

Not only has Konsa stepped in brilliantly for the injured Frenchman, but he has even proven to be just as good as Saliba was in Arsenal's title-winning season. Some areas of the data show Konsa has performed at higher levels.

But with Saliba now back in training and stepping up his fitness, Arteta has a task to balance the reintegration of one of his most important players, whilst keeping arguably their most in-form player happy.

And given the likes of Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City, Tottenham, Real Madrid and Manchester United face the Gunners before Christmas, these calls are important.

Konsa came to Arsenal with the reputation of being excellent at two key areas: accurate passing and duel-winning abilities. Since making the move from Villa to north London, he has continued that trend.

He ranks second in the Premier League this season for both passing accuracy and the percentage of ground duels won. These numbers make him one of the best defenders in the league this season in terms of an all-round game.

This form would normally make a player like Konsa undroppable at any level. The only issue is that one of the best centre-backs in the world is returning, who has been one of the centrepieces of the immense defensive unit Arteta has formed at the club.

The area that shows the importance of Saliba is the average height of Arsenal's defensive line. This season, without Saliba, the Gunners backline has dropped by at least one metre, no matter whether it is attacking or defending. It is a marginal shift, but this level has fine margins.

When Saliba broke into Arsenal's team in the 2022/23 season, Arsenal's defensive line was transformed. Their defensive line went higher by two metres compared to the previous season - partly due to the Frenchman's pace, with Saliba regularly described as a 'cheat code' in the way he can snuff out transitions and counter attacks with ease.

That higher line keeps opponents further away from their goal, leading to a better press and subsequently more Arsenal pressure and possession. Arteta regularly says one of the key aims for his team is "not allowing the opponent to breathe."

Konsa has done his fair share of sweeping up in the Arsenal high line this season. He has made three successful last-man tackles this season, with some of the highlights being result-defining challenges to deny the likes of Chelsea's Morgan Rogers and Nottingham Forest's Liam Delap as Arsenal protected one goal leads to claim victory.

But on that note, the centre-back partnership of Konsa-Gabriel has made more last-man tackles between them this season (seven), than Saliba-Gabriel needed in the whole of last season (five). Opponents are not just breathing a little, they are threatening in open spaces a bit more.

In a system where Arsenal pride themselves on giving next to nothing away in terms of attacking chances to their opposition, there is value in bringing back the 'cheat code'.

One scenario where Konsa and Saliba could play together is by moving the England international out to right-back, where he has played before in his career.

That would also suit Arteta's full-back plans - with the Arsenal manager almost exclusively playing natural full-backs in his full-back roles in recent years. Jurrien Timber, Ben White, Riccardo Calafiori and Piero Hincapie were all centre-backs by trade before moving to north London and being retrained as wider options.

However, the last couple of years has seen Konsa specialise centrally - to the point where he hasn't played a Premier League match at right-back for nearly two years.

His last league start as a full-back came in December 2024 when playing for Aston Villa, with his last 5,813 league minutes - the equivalent of nearly 65 games - coming as a centre-back. "Ezri, yeah, he can play as a full-back," said Arteta earlier this month. "I think his main position is as a centre-back."

And of course, Konsa and Saliba could play at centre-back together, giving Gabriel a bit of a rest when needed. It would mean moving one to a left centre-back role - and taking a left-footed centre-back out of the team, but the Arsenal manager is confident in that.

"He can play right or left," said Arteta of Konsa. "Willy has done the same with the national team and here at Arsenal. That's going to be something really positive for the team."

And while this could be a headache of Arteta, this has emerged as a positive problem. Arsenal have felt the impact of an injury to Saliba and Gabriel in the past - it has sometimes cost them Premier League and Champions League titles in recent years.

Now they're in a better place, but Arteta still has to get these big calls right. The Arsenal manager has sometimes made questionable selection calls this season in terms of the profiles he has in his team.

In the 3-0 loss at Brighton, he gave Bruno Guimaraes a first start in midfield when perhaps the more press-resistant Myles Lewis-Skelly was a better option against the high-intensity Seagulls in the press.

And in the recent win over Hull, Arteta went for Kai Havertz up front when the game was screaming out for Viktor Gyokeres' bullish nature against the three Tigers centre-backs.

Now Arteta has the a similar dilemma, only in defence.

#985. European shares join a global sell-off as AI spending fears rattle Wall Street and Asian markets

European shares have fallen after sharp losses in Asia and on Wall Street. Doubts over huge AI investments and fears of curbs following the Democrats' US midterm victory have rattled global markets.

European shares fell sharply in early trading on Friday as a global sell-off fueled by concerns over artificial intelligence stocks spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

Fears of curbs on AI data-center spending have added to investors' concerns after Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress.

The pan-European STOXX 600 index dropped 1.6% in early trading, wiping out its gains for the week. Most major European markets fell more than 1%, with media, healthcare and retail stocks leading the declines.

European markets had previously weathered the week's turbulence better than their Asian and US counterparts because of their more limited exposure to AI stocks.

Earlier, Japanese and South Korean shares tumbled after a massive selloff in tech stocks on Wall Street the previous day.

Tokyo's benchmark Nikkei 225 index fell 5.5% in early trade, while Seoul's tech-heavy Kospi index slid as much as 8.8%, triggering a circuit breaker which suspended trading for 20 minutes. Taiwan's benchmark TAIEX index was also down more than 8%.

Asian tech giants including Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) have borne the brunt of the artificial intelligence-related selloff.

Samsung plunged nearly 10% while SK Hynix slid over 11%.

Chip-related shares in Japan also took a beating, with Tokyo Electron stock trading down around 9% and Kioxia shedding 13%.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US markets were hammered on Thursday by a sharp retreat in tech stocks, particularly those involved in the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure like data centers.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.52% and shed as much as $2.5 trillion (roughly €2.23 trillion) in market value, while the broader S&P 500 index plunged 4.4%.

The rout occurred as investors grow increasingly anxious about the colossal AI spending plans and whether they will eventually produce commensurate profits.

The results of the US midterm elections, which saw Democrats seize control of both houses of US Congress, added to the concerns.

A number of Democratic governors-elect campaigned on slowing artificial intelligence development and promised to stop or pause the construction of data centers amid growing public opposition to such projects.

"It's pretty clear there's been a real shift ​in sentiment," Michael McCarthy, chief executive for Australia and New Zealand at online brokerage Moomoo, told the Reuters news agency.

"Market turning points are often accompanied by strong disagreement, and that shows up in the market ​by huge swings in either direction," he said. "That's what we appear to have had — and last night's emphatic sell-down suggests that is the direction that we're now headed in."

Despite Trey Nyoni's breakthrough this season, Liverpool are still light in the centre of the park

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Andoni Iraola's high press is yet to take its toll on the Liverpool squad after only 10 Premier League games, but there is every chance it will as the season wears on.

While the likes of Dominik Szoboszlai, Ryan Gravenberch and Alexis Mac Allister provide excellent press resistance and ball progression, for each of them to play 50-or-more games across all competitions in such a demanding system could prove untenable.

More urgent is that when the first wave of Liverpool's press is bypassed, the lack of a defensive shield leaves the backline exposed to central counter-attacks, which most notably occurred on the opening day of the new season against Newcastle.

If Liverpool are to maintain their competitive edge in the second half of the season, identifying a specialist No. 6 in the January transfer window is advisable.

According to a new data visualisation from Ballity Insight Lab analysing 68 LaLiga midfielders across the 2026/27 season, the profile Liverpool require is currently thriving in Spain. The below model plots 'duel destroyers' against 'ball-winners' seeking to find out which midfielders are good at both functions.

La Liga’s toughest midfielders? Duel Destroyer vs Ball Winner 📊 Wins it and wins duels: 🇦🇷 Guido Rodríguez, 🇪🇸 Rodri, 🇨🇴 Deossa, 🇫🇷 Camavinga, 🇪🇸 Gorrotxategi, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Bellingham, 🇩🇰 Hjulmand, 🇪🇸 Bernal, 🇫🇷 Lemar, 🇪🇸 Barrios Formula in the comments 👇 https://t.co/6rcVRo63vUNovember 16, 2026

The top-right quadrant of this scatter plot is categorised as the 'wins it and wins duels' bracket.

This zone is reserved for midfielders who consistently break up opposition play with lots of tackling and interceptions, whilst also dominating individual physical battles.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Unsurprisingly, the quadrant is populated by unattainable global stars such as Real Madrid duo Eduardo Camavinga and Jude Bellingham, alongside more established anchors like Guido Rodriguez and Morten Hjulmand.

However, just beneath those household names are two statistical outliers who could be January targets for the Anfield recruitment team: Jon Gorrotxategi and Nelson Deossa.

Gorrotxategi, who like Iraola is of Basque descent and currently represents Real Sociedad, stands out as the most compelling statistical fit for Liverpool’s needs.

The Spanish midfielder is positioned near the 95th percentile in the 'duel destroyer' category while simultaneously sitting around the 88th percentile as a ball-winner.

He boasts an aggressive, front-foot defensive style that would suit the demands of Premier League football.

The data suggests Gorrotxategi could function as Liverpool's midfield backstop, sweeping up loose balls and engaging opposition ball-carriers before they can reach the Reds' defensive third.

Deossa, meanwhile, presents an intriguing, slightly more balanced alternative, which perhaps Liverpool already have covered in their midfield stable.

The Colombian midfielder ranks just below the 90th percentile for ball-winning and hovers around the 85th percentile for duels. His profile suggests he is a player who reads the game well to block passing lanes, while retaining the physical bite required to win ground duels in the middle third.

Relying on converted No. 8s, or an up-and-coming 19-year-old, to anchor a title-challenging midfield is a compromise that opponents will punish as the season deepens. Liverpool need a player capable of holding central spaces when the full-backs push high and to win second balls from clearances.

The likes of Camavinga or Hjulmand may dominate mainstream transfer gossip columns this winter, but the smart money lies in targeting the anomalies.

In going for either Gorrotxategi or Real Betis man Deossa in January, Liverpool would acquire a midfield destroyer capable of plugging the gaps and protecting the defence, ultimately freeing their more technical midfielders to focus on unlocking opposition low blocks. Neither will come cheap, though, as both players are contracted to their respective clubs until June 2030.

#983. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

The Principality of Sealand is only half the length of a football pitch, but that hasn't stopped the tiny micronation from trying to make its grand return to international football.

In 1967, Major Roy Bates, the owner of a pirate radio station, occupied HM Fort Roughs – a fortress in the North Sea, seven miles off the Suffolk coast – and declared it a nation.

By 1975, Sealand had a flag, a constitution, an anthem and passports. Like any self-respecting country, it also needed a football team. The Sealand National Football

Association was first founded in 2003 – the entire national team was initially from Denmark, bizarrely – then revived by a Scot six years later, competing in non-FIFA matches against the likes of the Chagos Islands and Alderney. Fixtures weren't played on the offshore platform, but rather in Godalming, in Surrey. Royle Family actor Ralf Little was among those who played for the team, with former West Ham hard man Julian Dicks taking the coaching reins for a spell, before activities came to an end once more in the mid-2010s.

After a 12-year hiatus, Sealand is set to return in 2027 with both men's and women's ‘national sides', as well as a different approach.

“This team is all about spreading the message of Sealand, but we will be a proper international team ready to play other nations, both recognised and unrecognised,” director of football Ross Galbally tells FFT.

While it may appear that Sealand could struggle for a player pool (even Michael Bates, who inherited the platform from his dad, doesn't actually live there), anyone who takes up an e-citizenship of the Principality will be eligible for selection – that can be bought online for £7.99 a month, while noble titles are also available.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It costs £499.99 to become a Duke or Duchess, but just £39.99 to become a Baron or Baroness – in 2012, Ed Sheeran became Baron von Edward Sheeran of Sealand.

“Sealand's motto is ‘From the sea, freedom,'” Galbally explains. “Our team is open to anyone sharing our values. Every other country picks on citizenship and birthright, so why can't we select our team based on values?”

“THE WHOLE ADVENTURE IS ABOUT SEALAND AND ITS ETHOS, BUT ALSO THE PLAYERS' JOURNEYS”

The team's first trials will be held in early 2027, and people can apply from anywhere. There has already been interest from Argentina, the USA and Scandinavia.

“We hope Sealand will offer a second chance for players who missed out on showing their talent on the international stage,” Galbally says. “This whole adventure is about Sealand and its ethos, but also the players, their stories and their journeys.”

Sealand's managerial team is set to include coaches with experience in the EFL, as well as non-league. The executive board is a mixture of those with football backgrounds and people involved with music – a link to Sealand's pirate radio past.

The new team's inaugural game is likely to be in the UK, but matches could also take place in mainland Europe and the USA.

There are no plans to knock on FIFA or UEFA's door any time soon, and it also seems unlikely they'd meet the criteria to join CONIFA, the alternative organisation for nations, states and peoples not recognised by FIFA – current members of that organisation include Tibet, Greenland and Cornwall.

But Sealand has never been overly concerned about following the rules – from 2027, football's latest national side could be coming to a city near you.

#981. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

#980. Bancroft blows open Sandpapergate with extraordinary statement

Cameron Bancroft breaks silence on Sandpapergate and backs Usman Khawaja's claims entire Australia team knew about plan in South Africa in 2018; Bancroft says Pat Cummins' press conference denying any knowledge prompted him to speak out after being left feeling "angry, betrayed and alone"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Cameron Bancroft has directly accused Pat Cummins of knowledge of the use of sandpaper against South Africa in 2018.

In an explosive new 4,000-word statement in The West Australian newspaper, Bancroft has broken his silence on revelations in Usman Khawaja's new book, claiming that Cummins' press conference denying the allegations was the "final straw" for him, revealing that the entire bowling unit maintained full knowledge of the extensive use of sandpaper.

Bancroft saw his career turned upside after being suspended for his part in the incident alongside then captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner. Those were the only three players to be punished.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"It was not just the three of us - Steve Smith, David Warner and I - who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference.

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Bancroft's statement heaps the pressure on Test captain Cummins, with Australia's next red-ball series against New Zealand beginning on December 9.

The claims come in the wake of a furore of discussion around the 2018 scandal, with Khawaja's book first bringing to light claims that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper.

Khawaja also alleged that discussions about ball-tampering had been held "openly and lightheartedly" across the entire squad, involving not just the batters, bowlers and coaching staff but the wider team.

Those claims align with Bancroft's new statement, and with the recollection of former seamer Chadd Sayers, who also asserted that "everyone in that [2018] side" was aware of the ball-tampering plot.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Cummins called Khawaja's claims "complete and utter nonsense" in a sensational 68-minute press conference on Friday, with Starc also claiming "his recollection hadn't changed since 2021" when the bowlers released a joint statement denying knowledge.

The statement also comes just hours after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum to explore the scandal, stating that players could share their version of events without fears of reprisals - a decision which Khawaja and Warner have questioned.

Reacting to Bancroft, CA said in a statement: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.

"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.

"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."

Cummins' management then issued its own statement, which read: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."

Darren Lehmann - who was Australia head coach at the time of the scandal and named in Bancroft's statement as involved in discussions over the use of sandpaper - gave his own response to ABC radio, saying: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.

"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days. I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Bancroft's explosive statement alleges that the whole team would "laugh" about sandpaper and the game-changing effect it had on the Port Elizabeth Test match, where Australia took 4-28 in one session in the evening of day two. This was the second Test of the series, with Bancroft then being caught on camera in the third Cape Town Test.

"Not everyone was in the changing room at the time, but the conversation was not confined to Dave [Warner] and I," Bancroft continued.

"I was asked whether I could carry out the task. I felt uncomfortable and compromised. I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket.

"I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough. I also spoke with Tim Paine, who was in a key position behind the stumps to observe how the ball was moving.

"Everyone would laugh and speak about it sporadically on the field. We were all well aware of the riskiness of my behaviour. As time elapsed in that session there was excitement about the movement we were getting from the ball.

"There was an uncomfortable sense that something we all knew was wrong had become part of our effort to win the Test match. We took 4-28 in that final session. That is game changing!

"This was not something I did just once in the playing area after returning to the field from the tea break. This was an act I did nearly every over the whole last session on that day to begin with and then for the remainder of that Test match, up until I was caught in Third Test in Cape Town."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Bancroft's lengthy statement detailed the discussions around the use of sandpaper that took place in the changing room, in which he claims all players and coaches were present when media manager Kate Hutchinson made clear her opposition the players' plan to alter the ball.

"I remember my ball tampering with the sandpaper the evening before being discussed and my role being acknowledged in front of the group.

"Much like the celebrations when we took 4-28 the evening before, I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially [bowling coach] David Saker."

Saker resigned from the Australia set up in the wake of the scandal in 2019, before joining up with England's coaching team for the 2022 World Cup and 2023 Ashes.

"It reinforced the sense that what I was doing was being accepted as part of our collective effort," Bancroft continued.

"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening. I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion. I will never forget that.

"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing.

"She deserves the opportunity to give her own account. But her reaction is important because it completely challenges the idea that nobody had an opportunity to question what was happening. We did. I did. And I chose to continue."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Bancroft candidly reflected on the impact of the sandpaper scandal on his own international career. The batter has not made an appearance for Australia in seven years, with his last Test cap coming in the second Test of the 2019 Ashes.

"For eight years, I shared the burden of this story for the whole team," Bancroft added.

"This was a burden which was heavier than my capacity and I took the bullet for everybody, and it was my choice.

"My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019.

"But I have reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Bancroft also recalls the fallout in the dressing room once the use of sandpaper had been exposed on the big screen in Cape Town during the third Test against South Africa in 2018.

"After the match, I remember a lengthy meeting involving players and staff on the tour. We discussed how to respond to the scandal and the information that would need to be acknowledged publicly.

"By then, it was clear that the use of sandpaper could no longer be concealed. Nobody in that meeting stood up and said they had been completely unaware of my use of sandpaper. Not one person.

"Everyone started to give me advice about what I should say and what I shouldn't say to minimise the damage on the team related with the sandpaper saga.

"I had convinced myself that I was carrying out a role for the benefit of the team.

"Now I was facing the possibility that my international career might be over. As it turns out I ended up becoming the scapegoat for the entire team.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"Cummins said when directly asked the question: 'Were you aware of any ball tampering?' He said no.

"He could hide behind semantics and whether he knew sandpaper was being taken on the field that particular day or that particular session. But he directly said no.

"If you read The West Australian article from Bancroft, he says the media manager walked out because she was so unhappy with what was being discussed in a team meeting.

"How does the media manager know what's going on but a bowling unit doesn't?

"It would be the first time a bowling unit does not know what is happening to a cricket ball."

#979. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.
