#888. British TV Host Announces She's Pregnant at 59 During Live Broadcast

GB News co-host Renée Hoenderkamp revealed during a live broadcast that she is 12-weeks pregnant at 59 years old, nearly 40 years after giving birth to her first child.

This just in: Dr. Renée Hoenderkamp is pregnant at 59.

The British talk show anchor of GB News broke the news during a live broadcast that left her co-hosts stunned into silence.

As Hoenderkamp said in part during the Nov. 14 show, “I’m a mother of a grown-up boy and a very young girl. And I have some news to break to the panel today that they’re not aware of or anybody else for that matter: I’m actually going to be a mother of three shortly.”

Currently 12-weeks pregnant with a baby girl, the general practitioner is also mom to 37-year-old son Calum and 8-year-old daughter Alice.

Later in the show, Hoenderkamp explained how her fertility process began 18 months ago with the thought that she’d “like to do it again,” and eventually led her to travel to Poland to have her previously frozen eggs implanted.

But while the panelist is thrilled by her pregnancy news, she also detailed the commentary she previously faced for having her daughter at 50.

“I had criticism that I was selfish. What if I died in five years?” Hoenderkamp shared. “Well, you know I keep myself very fit, as you know. So hopefully that won’t happen, but it might.”

Still, she added, “My point is this: Alice has a wonderful life. She adores her life and I hope this child will be the same. What would be better? That they were never given the chance of life?”

Plus, Hoenderkamp—who will be 60 when her daughter arrives—sees her new baby as an opportunity to excel at parenthood the way she couldn’t do with her first child.

“At 21, I had youth on my side, but far less understanding of what motherhood required of me,” she wrote in an essay published in Daily Mail Nov. 17. “Nearly four decades later, while I have fewer years ahead of me, I also have the wisdom, patience and freedom to make the most of every moment.”

As Hoenderkamp sees it, “My new daughter will arrive into a family where she is desperately wanted, surrounded by people who already love her. In a world where much of our news is cause for enormous gloom, isn’t that something to celebrate?”

To learn what other notable figures have said about motherhood through the years, keep reading…

The Oscar winner, who has worked with organizations like UNICEF and is a UN Goodwill Ambassador, makes it a priority to share those same humanitarian values with her six children.

"With my family, I'm trying to raise them to have respect for all people and make friends around the world and feel at home with the world and really live a truly global [life]," she told NBC News in 2011. "I think it's what forms them and it's really important to me."

"I know it’s cliché, but I love everything, even the hard parts," the Kardashians star—mom to daughter True and son Tatum with ex Tristan Thompson—said of motherhood in a 2022 interview with Elle. "[My kids] challenge me as a person, and being able to shape little people into really incredible big people is an honor and a gift."

"We have to take those roles seriously, especially in today’s day and age, with how much accessibility children have and the information they’re exposed to so young," she added. "It’s super scary, but I take my job very seriously. I love it so much."

"I have such unconditional love for my kids," the Keep Up With the Kardashians alum—who shares North, Saint, Chicago and Psalm with ex-husband Kanye West—wrote on her website in 2017. "No matter what, I will always love them and support them in anything they choose to do in life."

"My family was so close growing up; now that I'm a mom, I understand the bond my mom and dad felt with us," she continued. "There can be ups and downs with kids but no matter what, I always learn so much from them. Being a mom is the most important job I have."

In a 2018 interview, the Kylie Cosmetics founder shared how much her mindset has changed since giving birth to Stormi that year.

"I think more about the future because of her. Every time I leave and I'm stressed about leaving her, I'm like, ‘I'm doing it for you,'" Kylie—who also shares son Aire with ex Travis Scott—told London Evening Standard. "Everyone says you change completely when you become a mom, but I really feel the same, just better."

The Poosh creator shares kids Mason, Penelope and Reign with ex Scott Disick. She's also mom to son Rocky with husband Travis Barker.

"It's definitely my favorite role in life," she said of motherhood in a 2012 interview with Parents. "It has changed me and made me realize there is nothing else I would rather do with my time. Being a mom is what life is about. I hope people realize what the priorities in life should be and know not everything has to be perfect."

As mom to kids Camden, Jaxon and Saylor with ex Jay Cutler, the Laguna Beach alum told Modeliste Magazine in 2016, "There's just so much more love in your life. I finally feel like I have a real identity"

"I feel like I have a purpose here in life now," she added. "I'm a mom to these three amazing little babies, and my whole world just kind of opened up."

"As soon as I found out I was pregnant," the Pretty Little Liars actress—who shares daughters Atlas and Rome with Matte Babel—said in a 2023 interview with Byrdie, "I put the old version of myself aside, and a new chapter began."

"I never want my children to say I work too much," she continued. "When I'm putting them to bed or having a meal with them, I put my phone down. They're growing up so quickly, and I don't want to look back and think, 'I missed this because of a work function.'"

The Lizzie McGuire alum is mom to son Luca with her ex-husband Mike Comrie. she also shares daughters Banks, Mae and Townes with husband Matthew Koma.

"I don't always balance it all," she admitted of her parenting duties in a 2018 interview with E! News, "I do the best that I can, and some months are crazier than others."

Still, Duff considers herself "a mother first."

"My decision-making process is like, 'Hey can I make this work?'" she said of finding family time in her busy work life. "I've been doing this for a while so I do have a strong work ethic, and I have a lot of people around me that help keep my schedule straight and plan and know where my priorities lie."

The powerhouse singer is a huge inspiration to all of us, but turns out the mother of Blue, Rumi and Sir—who she shares with husband Jay-Z—also makes sure to be the same for her own children.

"It just gives you purpose and all of the things that my self-esteem was associated it, it's all completely different," she said of motherhood in a 2012 interview with Anderson Cooper. "I realized why I was born and more than anything all of the things I want to pass onto my child and the best way of doing that is not by preaching or telling her but showing her by example."

For the Devil Wears Prada star, becoming a mom was a groundbreaking experience in both personal and work life.

“I don't think it's necessary to be a mother to play a mother. I think that should be open to lots of different actors," she told People in 2024, adding that welcoming sons Jonathan and Jack with husband Adam Shulman helped her gain an understanding of "the depth of love" maternal characters can feel.

The Mindy Project actress—who is mom to kids Katherine, Spencer and Anne—said she feels "so much more happy and confident after having children."

"In each subsequent year of my life, I'm just feeling happier and happier," she told ABC News in 2021, "and I am amazed at that,"

Though she played one of the titular Bad Moms in the 2016 comedy, the actress couldn't be a better parent to her kids Wyatt and Dimitri, who she shares with Ashton Kurcher.

"I reprioritized my life, in all honesty," Kunis said of her motherhood journey in a 2016 interview with Entertainment Tonight. "I traveled through all my 20s and I was very selfish—in a good way, not in a way I regret. And I think having a kid made me realize how incredibly selfless I want to be."

The Transformers actress—who shares kids Noah, Bodhi and Journey with her ex-husband Brian Austin Green, as well as daugther Saga with ex-fiancé Machine Gun Kelly—has a lovely approach to her parenting style.

"I don't think I need to teach my children with harsh words or with punishment. I believe that if I love them the right way, there's no need for that," she told Harper's Bazaar Arabia in 2015. "I'm a free-spirit mother."

The Gossip Girl alum and Ryan Reynolds' couple goals include being amazing parents to four children, including all the funny moments that come with being a parent.

"It's tough when you get pooped on and barfed on, but having a baby is wonderful," Lively joked to NW Magazine in 2016. "Even when it's tough and I'm exhausted, I think, 'I am so fortunate.'"

#887. Three Lions’ win over Spain comes in two acts: the first superb, the second heroic | Sid Lowe

Visitors take game to world champions and, though their hold on possession plummets, their rearguard is outstanding

In the final, absurdly tense moments before England finally did it and Spain finally fell, when Dan Burn had been sent on to do Dan Burn things, when the board had gone up with a 4 on but the clock wasn’t moving fast enough and the men in red kept coming back, Harry Kane had come to the side of the pitch to stand beside Thomas Tuchel. Palms out, Kane signalled and directed and appealed with his teammates to hold on to what they had: somehow, anyhow. What they had was special, but their grip on it was not as secure as it had seemed. Not as secure as it should have been too.

Tuchel gave Kane a nudge that looked pretty playful considering the pressure, before Marc Bollengier, the fourth official, ordered him back to the bench. But England’s captain was not gone for long and when he returned he was joined by almost all of them, awaiting the big moment. From there, he watched James Trafford make an astonishing double save, a moment of heroism that allowed them to hang on. Then, standing alongside the rest who could no longer just sit there, he saw the last header clear – Dan Burn things – before the whistle went. Then he and they went on one last run, back on to the pitch.

As they went there was celebration for them, applause for all of them, Spain too. What a game it had been, what a night. “We knew we would beat them,” Declan Rice claimed afterwards. Would? Maybe in the 60th minute they had known, England 3-0 up and playing their way to a superb and, yes, comfortable victory over the world champions – the first team to beat them, penalties aside, in 44 games and almost a thousand nights. But with half an hour left Spain had been revived, England reduced to 10 men and, as Tuchel said: “Thirty minutes against Spain feels like three hours.”

It did to him, to his players too. To everyone else, it flew by. This is the best game you can see in football, Spain’s head coach, Luis de la Fuente, had said, and he wasn’t wrong. When England got that third, the fans had sung: “You’ve seen the England, now eff off home.” Nah, you’re all right, thanks. Far better to stay and watch this; it had been hugely impressive from England; now, here were Spain too. Now, it was going to be wild. Nervy, noisy and fun.

Jarell Quansah lost the ball, Fermín López released Lamine Yamal and Spain won a penalty that Mikel Oyarzabal scored. It was some game. Twice Spain scored; countless times they came, the Metropolitano chanting: “Yes, we can!” In the end, they could not, but they had got close. They had really believed they might; as the momentum built, perhaps they had really believed they would.

This was history: made by England, perhaps; broken by England, certainly. Spain had not been beaten in 90 or 120 minutes since Colombia defeated them two and a half years ago, their only loss in that period coming on penalties against Portugal in last year’s Nations League final. They had not lost a competitive game since Scotland in March 2023. That, Fifa said, was the longest run ever and even if there was an asterisk, it was still mightily impressive, but it had to end some time. If not necessarily like this.

“With every passing game, defeat gets closer,” De la Fuente said. Now, it arrived. “They can seem invincible but we’re ready,” Tuchel had said. At the end Spain’s staff lined up to applaud their players off. England’s players stood before their fans, exhausted, arms raised.

Italy went into their clash in Brussels top of Group A1 after their 3-1 win against France on Thursday but came crashing back to Earth as they were comfortably beaten by Belgium.

Pio Esposito gave Italy ⁠an early lead but their joy was short-lived as Belgium scored ​three times before the ​interval through Maxim De Cuyper, ​Nathan Ngoy and Jérémy Doku (pictured). Diego Moreira made it 4-1 in the 80th minute.

France beat Turkey 2-1 in Bordeaux ​thanks to an own ‌goal by Emirhan ​Topcu and ​an effort by Bournemouth's Eli Junior Kroupi, meaning they won the group with 13 points, ahead of Belgium who ended on 12. Italy, on 10 points, missed out.

England and Spain had already confirmed qualification to the quarter-finals before Sunday's dramatic clash between the sides in Madrid, which England won 3-2, but the remaining match in Group A3 saw Croatia beat Czechia 2-1, thanks to Lovro Majer's 87th-minute winner.

In Group C1, Albania sealed top spot and promotion to League B after a 2-0 win over Belarus in Budapest. Rey Manaj and Elseid Hysaj scored goals in each half. Finland ended their campaign in the group with a 7-2 thumping of San Marino in Helsinki, headlined by a hat-trick by forward Adrian Svanbäck. San Marino are relegated to League D after failing to register a single point from their six games, ending with a goal difference of -22.

In Group C2, Montenegro completed an unbeaten group campaign with a 4-1 victory in Cyprus. Genoa forward Milutin Osmajic got them off to a fast start in the fifth minute while Nikola Krstocic added a second-half double. Armenia and already-relegated Latvia played out a goalless draw in Riga. Reuters and Guardian sport

Ultimately, this came in two acts. The first act was superb from England, the second heroic. “We can’t play like them and they can’t play like us,” De la Fuente had said and yet what was so striking about the way that this began was that England took the game to Spain on their own terms. They were the ones dominating the ball, not allowing their opponents out; theirs was the midfield, the control.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Ten minutes is not a reliable sample size it is true – and it turned out even an hour might not have been enough – but as the clock rolled into double figures, the possession stat showed 70% for England. While that number fell, when it reached 20 the shot count was 4-0. The first came after 39 seconds and before Spain had a touch, Unai Simón flashing out a right hand to Jude Bellingham’s shot inside the six-yard box. Martín Zubimendi immediately had to stop Anthony Gordon’s shot and then Simón stopped Rice. All that inside three minutes; three more and Kane was flashing a shot just wide.

England’s fans were enjoying this. A chorus of “the best in the world, the best in the world, Harry Kane, the best in the world” came down. They watched England control Spain’s place, Elliot Anderson and Rice excelling. They watched England take the lead, Kane scoring his 93rd goal with penalty No 28. They watched Bellingham burst through, responding by launching into a rendition of the Beatles which was still going when they watched Ezri Konsa head in the second. Then they watched Bellingham burst through again to set up Ben White. They watched England be brilliant for an hour but there was still plenty of Spain to watch as well. Nervously now and they will remember Trafford’s superhero rescue for some time, but it was still their night, and what a night.

#886. 'Why not have a go?' - the halfway line goal phenomenon

Diego Gomez's shot against Crystal Palace soars over Walter Benitez

David Beckham's goal from the halfway line against Wimbledon in 1996 is one of football's iconic moments.

It helped to catapult the Manchester United midfielder to global stardom and remains a staple of highlight reels.

The impudence to shoot from such a distance highlighted the exceptional talent and character of the future England captain.

Premier League players are now trying their luck from long range more regularly, testing their instinct, precision and technique.

Diego Gomez's stunning 51-metre (56-yard) strike for Brighton against Crystal Palace last month added to the spectacular list in the Premier League, while players in the EFL and FA Cup have contributed their own.

There have already been 19 attempts from over 50 metres this season, on course to beat last season's Premier League total of 26.

Of the 2,733 shots in the Premier League this term, 0.7% of them have come from over halfway - up on 0.3% over the course of last season.

This sample size is admittedly small. And in the case of goals scored from distance lower down the football pyramid, this is data that isn't readily available.

But why are we seeing a growing number of shots being taken from such extravagant distance?

Gomez tried to score from deep in his own half during Brighton's 2-0 win at Sunderland on 10 October.

A week later, he beat Walter Benitez with the longest-range goal in the Premier League since Wayne Rooney's 57.6m strike for Everton against West Ham in 2017.

The Paraguayan took advice from Lionel Messi, when the pair were at Inter Miami, to always look to play the ball forward to another level.

It is not just Premier League players who are trying their luck from outrageous distances.

Charlie McNeill scored from halfway for Crewe in their recent 2-1 FA Cup win against AFC Wimbledon.

The on-loan Sheffield Wednesday forward, who played once for Manchester United before leaving Old Trafford in 2024, beat goalkeeper Joe Bursik to open the scoring.

Having done it while at Manchester City and Manchester United's academies, the 23-year-old felt his latest attempt was instinctive.

He told BBC Sport: "Goalies nowadays are always quite high up the pitch - playing a sweeper-keeper role - and I always have a thought if I ever got into that situation to have a go.

"You see it more and more. I had the opportunity so I thought: 'Why not have a go?'

"It was one of those goals. I turned and saw him off his line and in that split-second made the decision to shoot.

"I knew I caught it sweetly and I was following it the whole way in so I knew it had a good chance, but as the keeper was going back I thought he was going to get it.

"When I watched it back it dropped quite early, but as it was getting closer and closer I thought it was going to go over because it went quite high but it dropped in."

Crewe Alexandra's Charlie McNeill talking about the rise in halfway line goals

McNeill joins a growing number of players to have scored from the halfway line or inside their own half over the past 18 months.

Preston Fearon, now on loan at Forest Green, scored two goals from around the halfway line for West Ham Under-21s in their win against Burnley last month.

Gbemi Arubi was barely a stride over the halfway line when he scored for Burton against Peterborough in October.

Last season, Abdul Fatawu (Leicester), Ryan Ledson (Huddersfield), Reyes Cleary (Barnsley), Regan Hendry (Mansfield) and Sammy Braybrooke (Newport) all scored from the halfway line or inside their own half in the EFL.

Two years ago, Chelsea's Moises Caicedo scored from the centre circle against Bournemouth.

Is it all about the goalkeeper's position, as they stand higher up the pitch to either stop opposition attacks or get their own team moving?

"You've got to execute it properly, but it plays a big part. Most keepers are like that, high out the net, because we are playing over the top so they are there first, to get the ball," said McNeill.

"I have always had it in my head and have tried it a couple of times. Although it's not like I do my homework and see he is always off his line. It's one of those instinctive moments."

Paul Robinson scored two goals in his career, one for Tottenham and one for Leeds

Asmir Begovic holds the record for the longest-range Premier League goal when the goalkeeper scored from 95.7m for Stoke against Southampton in 2013.

Two other goalkeepers have scored from their own half: Tim Howard for Everton against Bolton in 2012 and Paul Robinson, who netted for Tottenham against Watford in 2007.

Yet they were flukes rather than by design - similar to Barrow goalkeeper Ben Winterbottom's goal from his own half in their 3-0 National League win at Gateshead on Saturday.

Robinson, who also scored for Leeds against Swindon in 2004, external, feels conceding from distance is now a risk managers are willing to take.

The former England international said: "We've seen the game evolve in the way where the goalkeeper becomes a key figure in starting a pattern of play. The manager wants the goalkeeper at the base of the back three, four or five.

"But then also we're seeing a lot more teams playing with a higher line and the goalkeeper then has to take a higher line of starting position to read the through ball.

"When your team are playing a high line, you obviously have to be further up the field and you're concentrating on where your defensive line is, as opposed to where the football is at times.

"It's one of those things modern-day managers are willing to accept if and when it does happen, because of the way they want their goalkeeper to play.

"We see so many managers come out now and say: 'It's OK. I'm quite happy with them making mistakes. This is the way I want them to play. Blame me because that's what I've asked them to do.'

"We're probably entering that type of territory with it."

With attackers aware of the higher starting position of opposing keepers - a result of teams pressing high - and likely to have been encouraged by the success of other long-range efforts across football, attempts from extreme distance are becoming more frequent in the Premier League this season.

The conversion of efforts from more than 50 metres have increased too - up to 5.3% this season, compared to 1.1% across the previous three seasons combined, with Gomez's strike the first Premier League goal scored from over 50 metres since the 2023-24 season.

It's a small sample size, so more time is required for clearer trends, at least in the Premier League to be established.

But with more long shots being taken and keepers starting higher, there is a suggestion (and hope) we may see more Goal of the Season contenders before the term is out.

#885. Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’

Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them

In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.”

With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week.

Two days earlier Tenerife had been in Navahermosa, La Mancha, the tiny village their teammate’s family are from, carrying the coffin of the friend their captain called “our Demigol”. They were supposed to be in Granada on Saturday; instead, they were back on the island, in their home ground, to say goodbye and pay homage. Publicly, this time. Lilies had been laid on the pitch there too, a Tenerife shirt with them, and a stage built at one end. “We’ve seen how fragile life is,” the captain, Enric Gallego, said, offering words he said could never be enough, carrying the burden for all of them. “We think of the journeys, the wins, the losses, and hold on to those moments that seemed normal, but that now … a few days ago we shared that with you. To talk of you in the past tense is unfair. None of us are prepared to live what we’re living through.”

No one ever could be. Across Spain this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them. That, Budimir had told his teammates, was something they must think about but not think about too. The players’ union in which De Miguel had a role, a footballer there for others, had asked for the competition to stop. Respect demanded that it did, they said, requesting a judge intervene when the league did not hear them. But it had gone on. The only matches postponed were those involving Tenerife; Andorra, whose goalkeeper Jesús Owono had crashed into De Miguel; and Castellón, who he had taken to the second division, delivering them to segunda for the first time in 16 years and himself for the first time at all, aged 27.

On the eve of the game that opened this weekend’s fixtures, the Sevilla head coach, Luis García, said he thought they should wait. It was too soon, too raw, too theirs. His midfielder Giorgi Kochorashvili had missed training the day before: a former Castellón player, Kochorashvili had asked permission to go to the funeral, leaving early and returning late, his mind elsewhere. Of course he could, García had replied, “we are humans above all else”. And it was not just him. García had worked with Owono – “let’s not make two victims, we have had enough; he is in hell, for sure”, he had pleaded – and now he said: “If there’s a play that’s similar … what do I say to my goalkeeper?

“We need time,” García had said. “We need to reflect.”

Instead, they played. From Seville on Friday night to Madrid on Sunday, via stadiums everywhere. It was, some suggested, the best way to pay homage to De Miguel but no one truly knew. “We can’t ask him what he would have wanted,” José Mourinho said before Madrid went to Valencia and won 3-0, Tenerife’s flag flying at half-mast at Mestalla. He might not have wanted anything at all. “You never wanted any attention,” Gallego said, but this weekend he was on all their minds.

“Forever in our memories,” the league’s line read. At every game in the first and second divisions, the ritual was repeated. Teams came out together wearing the same white shirts bearing his name. Flowers were laid, a little uncomfortably, on the spot inside the centre circle where he had fallen and there was a minute’s silence, players and officials gathered around the wreath. As they stood before Cádiz-Oviedo, tears ran down the cheeks of the Tenerife-based referee Marta Huerta de Aza. On stadium screens, an image of De Miguel appeared. On television screens, a QR code did: a link to a crowdfunding campaign for the young family he left, set up by the former Tenerife player Fran Sol.

The games began and then, in the ninth minute or as near as the referee could manage, they paused again: the teams stopped, looking up to the screen, where a video of his best moments played out. It was not always an easy watch, and some preferred not to.

At Sevilla, where fans saw Antonio Puerta collapse on the pitch and pass away, applause still offered in the 16th minute every game, Kochorashvili stood by the bench, eyes lost somewhere his mind was not. At Espanyol, where in the 21st minute they applaud Dani Jarque, the captain who died during a pre-season tour and to whom Andrés Iniesta dedicated the winning goal at the 2010 World Cup final, Álex Calatrava and Álvaro González, teammates at Castellón and Tenerife respectively, looked about to break. In the ninth minute at the Metropolitano, the place was still rocking, the timing out of sync: Giuliano Simeone had just scored, so the referee Javier Alberola Rojas allowed a couple of minutes to pass, choosing his moment, Diego Simeone helping him impose silence on the stands when he finally stopped it. Then they started again, expected to carry on regardless.

In Pamplona, Alejandro Catena, who scored the late equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Athletic, raised an Osasuna shirt with De Miguel’s name and number on the back. Theirs was the game that felt most out of place, attention drawn from where it should have been, where it was. It would not be true to say that it did not matter, the Osasuna head coach, Jagoba Arrasate, admitting he had been carried along with it like everyone else, the calmness he thought they had found in the months out of the game soon abandoned again.

As they played, grateful for the grand day that they had before them, all the days they did, the tribute continued in Tenerife. The Heliodoro had filled early, access by every gate except eight and nine, engulfed by flowers and candles. De Miguel’s shirt lay on the turf where he had, lilies to one side, a spotlight on it. Another wreath occupied the bench. A giant shirt stretched across one end where the stage was, a lectern awaiting the speakers. A cross presided over it. Staff and players wore No 9 badges on their lapels. Supporters came in Tenerife shirts. And in the yellow shirts of rivals Las Palmas, whose president and captain Kirian, who had recovered after cancer, came. “This is the Canaries I want,” said Tenerife’s majority shareholder, Rayco García.

In the seats set up on the pitch, Tenerife’s players and De Miguel’s family sat, their eyes heavy. The archbishop, Eloy Alberto Santiago led a mass. The club’s president and majority shareholder spoke. He promised they would never allow María, De Miguel’s widow, to be alone. He also announced they would adopt Carla, his 14-month-old daughter, supporting her economically until she is 18. Gallego addressed her, football as family meaning something. “I hope one day you can look back and see who your dad was, be proud of him, not just for the footballer he was but the person: for his humility, his goodness,” he said.

Sniffing, his voice breaking, the captain paid homage to his teammate, his strike partner, his friend. The kind of person, he said, who did not seem to be there, and definitely did not demand that people notice he was, but always was. A man, he noted, so disinclined to put anyone out that when his car broke down he walked home from training rather than bother anyone for a lift. That, he insisted, might not seem like much, but it said much. “Today we don’t want to talk only of the player; we want to talk about you, Jesús, about the person that was behind the shirt,” he had begun. “Above any game, any team, what really remains is the person and the impact you leave. And you were a very special person.”

Gallego gave way to the archbishop, orations led by Tenerife staff, and as the act came to a close, difficult days ahead, the spotlight taken elsewhere, the drums began and the fans belted out a familiar tune, once more with more meaningful than ever before:

double quotation markWe have to sing with even more strength if you’re losing Even those who left us sing, from heaven This will never stop We will sing to eternity.”

Then Tenerife’s players departed. They have training on Monday and next week they play.

#883. Mauricio Pochettino asked the US to believe in his project. Did he believe in it himself?

The coach’s tenure with the USMNT brought a whiplash of highs and lows. He met some goals but also left many with the impression he never truly bought in

It did not take US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino very long to take his first big swing.

He’d just taken the reins of the program after a disastrous performance at the 2024 Copa América cost his predecessor his job, with the first home World Cup in three decades looming on the horizon. The federation introduced him in New York City, on the 24th floor of a building overlooking the Hudson River. In short order, he was asked about the culture surrounding the program. In his answer, he invoked the four-time World Cup champion US women.

“We need to believe that we can win,” Pochettino said that day in September 2024. “That we can win not only a game: We can win the World Cup.”

It is the type of belief that feels almost alien to observers of the US men, the type of statement that American fans yearn to hear so badly from a coach yet also roll their eyes at. For years, fans of men’s soccer in the US have been desperate to taste glory, and for years they have developed an inferiority complex spurred along not only by results but by international perception. Even in the present day, with American players playing in Europe at the very highest level, the idea that the US could win a men’s World Cup feels borderline preposterous.

That never stopped Pochettino from espousing his belief that the US should believe they could make a miraculous run in 2026 and win the whole thing. It was a mantra he returned to frequently during his time leading the team, publicly and privately, even in the weeks leading up to the tournament. Pochettino even told Donald Trump that the US could win it all, perhaps planting the seeds for an assist turned own-goal down the line.

Belief is something that could attract even the most casual US fans, the type of newcomers whose previous experience with an American soccer coach came from Apple TV. Unfortunately for US fans, Pochettino’s actions never quite lined up with the inspirational speech.

There was the near-constant stream of rumors attaching Pochettino to clubs in England, rumors he never really went out of his way to quash even before they tied him to the Manchester United job he has now accepted. In many ways this type of thing is unavoidable and understandable: bringing on a high-profile coach and expecting peace and quiet is the footballing equivalent of dating a supermodel and expecting no one else to make an advance. Yet too often it felt as if Pochettino was the one stoking the fire; it was not uncommon to wake up in the States and find social media feeds populated with clips of the Argentinian espousing the valor of the Premier League and even floating the idea of returning someday.

This was never really shocking or unexpected and was far from offensive. Professional sports are fickle and players, coaches and administrators alike are wise to keep their options open and their bridges intact. Yet it was a bit galling to hear from someone brought in to galvanize the US’s players and fans ahead of a generational event: a home World Cup.

Pochettino also seemed sometimes frustrated by the very thing he was in part brought in to help change: American soccer’s sometimes awkward place in America itself. After losing the 2025 Gold Cup final to Mexico in Houston, he went out of his way to criticize the idea that the US would play in front of a pro-Mexico crowd on home soil, an issue that predates Pochettino by decades and may well never be solved, one even the most cursory research would’ve revealed prior to arrival. He fairly criticized the lack of stakes in Major League Soccer and suggested that US players are coddled throughout their youth development while at the same time butting heads with media who dared question the effects of a group-stage loss to Turkey at this summer’s World Cup. In reality, he faced far less pressure as the head coach of the USMNT than he would have in most any other major footballing nation.

All of it too often gave observers the feeling that Pochettino was never truly bought in. But then, there was the whiplash, which was palpable. As soon as one began to feel that way, there’d be a fresh injection of dopamine – the US’s 4-1 demolishing of Paraguay, for example, far and away their best-ever performance at a World Cup. And there was Poch, nearly in tears and belting out Country Roads, then speaking glowingly about America, American football and everything else that comes along with it. A few weeks later, they’d suffer a 4-1 drubbing at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 that will go down as among the worst-ever performances by the US at a World Cup. Certainly the most traumatic.

Athletes and coaches hate being asked about their legacies, in general. The question in and of itself sounds moribund, as if the person asked is about to ascend into the ether. Legacies, too, are tricky things – they often take years to materialize, and they’re sometimes just as quickly erased by shifting perceptions or the accomplishments of successors.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Pochettino does not seem to be the kind of person who would mind being asked about his legacy; he actually seems more like one who would already have one in mind before departure. Yet when asked by the Guardian on Friday to define his lasting impact, he struggled to do so at first. “I am not arrogant,” Pochettino replied with a smile and a laugh. “Well, not arrogant enough. I am a little bit arrogant.”

Eventually he relented. Pochettino’s lasting impact, the coach said, was largely down to relationships, to having done things the right way, in his mind.

“The most valuable feeling that we get isn’t one victory, or that we helped in the program,” he said. “It is that relationship in the program – even when you cross the sea, you look and smile because I think you share the values that are very important in life, more important than anything else. That is our principal that we respect always.”

Pochettino has always thought in big, broad, ambitious strokes and has executed those visions over the course of his career with varying degrees of success. In the United States, he arrived with varying goals: ensure a proper showing at a home World Cup, help change the perception of the game to the general public and lay down roots for long-term growth.

In some ways, Pochettino certainly succeeded. In others, he’s left the whole of American soccer wanting. It’s a fitting end for a coach who wanted so many people to believe – yet might never have felt that way himself.

#882. Nick Cannon, Moms of His 12 Kids Reveal Dynamic in Raising the Cannons

Nick Cannon—dad to twins Moroccan and Monroe with Mariah Carey and 10 children with five women—unveiled his life as a father of 12 on his new Netflix show.

Nick Cannon's family is experiencing growing pains.

The Drumline star, who is dad to 12 children, is letting fans inside his life as the head of a blended family through his upcoming docuseries Raising the Cannons.

"I have a relationship with six women and 12 children," Cannon explained in the trailer for the Netflix show, debuting Dec. 18. "This is a world that I created, and I have to deal with everything that comes with it."

And Cannon—who first became a dad after welcoming twins Moroccan and Monroe, 15, with ex Mariah Carey—has learned co-parenting can be difficult given the complex rapport between him and his partners (He’s also dad to Golden Sagon, 9, Powerful Queen, 5 and Rise Messiah, 4, with Brittany Bell, twins Zion Mixolydian and Zillion Heir, 5, and Beautiful Zeppelin, 4, with Abby De La Rosa, Halo Marie, 3, and as well as a late son, Zen, with Alyssa Scott, Legendary Love, 4, with Bre Tiesi and Onyx Ice, 4, with LaNisha Cole.)

As such, the Wild 'n Out creator—who according to Netflix is romantically involved with De La Rosa, Scott and Tiesi—explained, "I want my children to have relationships with one another. One day we all would be able to get along."

Yet Cole expressed acting as one big happy family is a performance she's not willing to put on for the cameras.

"I don't need to create this false narrative," the photographer said in confessional, "like we're one big happy family when we're not."

Meanwhile, De La Rosa had her own take on her partner's role in creating challenges between the women in his life. In her words narrating the trailer offscreen, "Nick formulates these worlds as if we're so separate. Everyone thinks it's competition. No, it's our reality."

For her part, Tiesi, who also stars on Selling Sunset, objected to the notion that she and her son had to fight for Cannon's attention, stating to cameras, "I am not in competition," while also appearing to tell Cannon on the phone the other matriarchs in their circle "broke, pathetic losers."

As for how the comedian's kids feel about their unique family dynamic? Both Moroccan and Monroe chimed in with concerns for their father, who admitted his ego sabotaged his six-year marriage with their mom, Carey, which ended in 2014.

"If you didn't have all these kids," Monroe told Cannon, "you would have been back together," referring to the Grammy winner. In turn, her twin brother suggested in their joint confessional that their dad's lifestyle was not "sustainable in any way."

Need a bird's-eye view of Cannon's expansive family tree? Keep reading...

Children No. 1 and 2: Moroccan Cannon and Monroe Cannon

Mariah Carey gave birth to her and Nick's twins on April 30, 2011. The two announced their split in 2015 after six years of marriage and finalized their divorce a year later.

Beauty queen Brittany Bell gave birth to her and Nick's first child together, a boy, on Feb. 21, 2017.

Brittany and Nick welcomed their second baby together, a girl, in December 2020.

DJ Abby De La Rosa gave birth to her and Nick's twin boys on June 14, 2021.

Model Alyssa Scott welcomed a baby boy with Nick on June 23, 2021.

However, just five months after the arrival of their son, Nick shared the devastating news that Zen had passed away from brain cancer. "Alyssa was just the strongest woman I have ever seen," he said on the Dec. 7 episode of The Nick Cannon Show. "Never had an argument, never was angry. She was emotional when she needed to be but was always the best mom and continues to be the best mom possible. So I've got to say thank you to my entire family but specifically to Alyssa."

"You never know what someone is going through," he added. "Hug your family. Kiss somebody. Tell them you love them."

Model Bre Tiesi welcomed her first child with Nick on June 28, 2022. The baby boy weighed 8 pounds and 10 ounces at birth.

"I did it. An all natural unmedicated home birth," Bre shared in a July 2022 Instagram post. "This was the most humbling / limit pushing yet awakening and completely empowering experience. I can't thank my team enough for delivering my son safely."

Nick and model LaNisha Cole welcomed a daughter on Sept. 14, 2022.

Abby gave birth to a baby girl, her third child with Nick, in November 2022.

The model shared an Instagram video showing the Wild 'n Out star helping to deliver their baby. "Our lives are forever changed," she wrote. "Zen is in every breath I take. I know his spirit was with us in the room that morning. I know he is watching down on us. He shows me signs everyday. I will hold onto this memory forever."

She continued, "I will remember the sound of Nicks voice saying 'it's a girl' and the look of everything we've been through flash across his face. I will remember the sound of her crying out with her first breath and feeling her heartbeat against mine. My sweet girl, I got my surprise!! We love you Halo Marie Cannon!"

#881. Iran war oil shock drives dip in global emissions, study shows

Global carbon emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but not because of major progress on climate action. Instead, it's high energy prices following the US attack on Iran that's driving the trend.

Global carbon emissions are set to slightly drop this year, a new study suggests, largely as a result of high energy prices in the wake of the US war on Iran and the disruption of supply through the Strait of Hormuz.

Emissions from oil, gas and coal are the main drivers of climate change. While over the past decade, these emissions have risen by 0.9% per year, they are expected to drop by 0.4% in 2026.

"It's downwards, which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what's happened in the Strait of Hormuz," said the study's co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway.

"So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons."

The study was released while global leaders are meeting in Turkey for the United Nations' COP31 climate conference.

The study published by international research group the Global Carbon Project found that oil emissions dropped by 1.9% in 2026, while natural gas fell by 0.3%. Coal emissions however continued to rise, by around 0.6%.

"A drop in emissions in ‌one year is not a peak unless it ‌is driven ​by structural change," Peters cautioned.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A structural change would mean that emissions would slowly rise to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, indicating a long term trend. That's not what happened though, Peters said. "What we see this year is [that] oil emissions are going up and then suddenly, bang, down 2%."

It is the third time in recent years that global carbon pollution has dropped. The previous declines were during the global economic crisis in 2009 and during the COVID pandemic in 2020. In each of those cases, emissions went back up once global economies recovered.

While the geopolitical shocks of the past year have been the driving factors behind the temporary emissions reversal, there has also been a rise in renewable energy contributing to the data. So while solar panels, wind farms and electric vehicles did make a difference, they were just not enough to cut emissions by themselves.

"The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies," according to co-author of the study, Pierre Friedlingstein, of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University.

And even though emissions from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions still went up by about 1%, the study warns. The overall rise is because of land use changes like deforestation and peat fires, which increased too fast to be offset by the slight decrease in fossil fuel burning.

#879. Familiarity of Doha drives home just how far Socceroos have come in recent years | Joey Lynch

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality, highlighted by a return to the scene of Asian Cup heartbreak

Last week’s 3-0 dismissal of Qatar at the Abdullah bin Khalifa Stadium marked the first time the Socceroos had returned to the Gulf state since their heartbreaking elimination from the Asian Cup just under three years ago. Back then, coach Graham Arnold called Doha a “home away from home” after they relocated there during the Covid pandemic, and went so far as to suggest that they would have some form of advantage at the 2022 World Cup as a result.

Wandering around the city in 2026, memories rush back of Socceroos fans becoming eager participants in the takeover of the city’s souks during the World Cup. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. It evokes recollections of trips on the red Metro line out to the Al Janoub Stadium in Al Wakrah, aided by the faded posters and stickers celebrating the 2022 tournament’s arrival that to this day can still be seen in shopfronts. There’s the excitement, for some, when a stray cat reminds you just how personable the local felines can be, as well as the sense of unease that remains whenever one pauses to reflect on how all this was built and the hands that did so.

But for all the familiarity and continuity for the Socceroos – five players who were there when Son Heung-min broke Australian hearts featured in Friday’s win – being back in Doha rams home just how much has changed for this team, and how well and truly into a new era we are.

Tony Popovic occupies the dugout these days, after the defeat to Korea arguably represented the beginning of the end of Arnold’s tenure by sparking a fatigue that would culminate in a downturn in results and his resignation later that year.

Nestory Irankunda, the rapidly emerging star of Popovic’s team who now has eight international goals to his name, was about to suffer a 4-0 defeat against the Central Coast Mariners nearly three years ago. Alessandro Circati was left out of the Socceroos squad to ensure he retained his place in the Parma side seeking to secure promotion to Serie A. Paul Okon-Engstler, Patrick Beach and Lucas Herrington were all yet to play senior football.

These players, who all started against Qatar, are emerging cornerstones of a new Socceroos setup that fielded the World Cup’s youngest side in North America, before flashing signs of further growth against Brazil in September. On Friday, this talented group bullied the two-time defending Asian champions on their own turf in the first-half, putting the game to bed before Popovic swung the changes and things got disjointed after half-time.

There is increasing evidence of an evolution not only in approach but also mentality. Of players bringing to the national team the lessons they’ve learned not just in the green and gold, but also in their experiences at bigger, more demanding clubs and leagues – in part because of the platform they’ve been offered by Popovic.

All of which could make it serendipitous if Tuesday’s game against Jordan, at the symbolic home of his predecessor, proves to be the end of the Popovic era.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

The players aren’t going anywhere but with his contract situation still up in the air, it could well prove to be Popovic’s last game in charge of the Socceroos if he doesn’t agree to an extension. Given the postponement of January’s Asian Cup, there may not be the send-off he might have envisioned. Instead, a 12,000-seat stadium – unlikely to be very full – will host a hastily relocated friendly that’s entire raison d’être has vanished.

Remarkably, after sensitive discussions to relocate Tuesday’s game after player resistance to travelling to Amman, in line with DFAT advice, Doha could once again be pressed into action to serve as a historic backdrop for the Socceroos, just as a pandemic already saw it become the site of many a moment of distinction.

#877. A long wait, some magic and that smile: Ronaldinho savours Ravenna debut at 46

Brazilian legend, an investor at Serie C club, showed glimpses of old brilliance as he played 45 minutes for the promotion-chasing side

It may have been the longest buildup in world football. In June, the former Barcelona and Brazil legend Ronaldinho was unveiled by the Serie C side Ravenna to make his comeback at the age of 46 – 11 years after his last official game. Then silence.

But on a chilly November day on the eastern coast of Italy, there he was, not only in the squad, but in the starting XI for the eagerly anticipated derby against Forlì as Ravenna chase promotion.

The Ravenna manager, Andrea Mandorlini, deployed Ronaldinho in a central position, just behind the striker Simone Rabbi. The Brazilian held his position well, but was slow to get going. As the game progressed, he warmed up and showed his excellent skills; some things do not appear to change. Ronaldinho touched the ball 25 times, took three corners – one of which nearly led to a Ravenna goal – and initiated the move that led to the hosts taking the lead in the 35th minute.

Having trained with the team just once, whether he plays again remains to be seen. But he had already sprinkled some magic on a club and a region that has not made headlines in years. He played the first half as Ravenna won 2-0 to stay second in the division’s Group B (the Italian third tier is divided into three regional sections). Only the group winners earn promotion and Ravenna trail Spezia by six points.

Whatever happens for the remainder of the season this has put the club back on the football map. Ravenna’s highest finish was eighth in Serie B, in 1996-97, but this match was broadcast live by Sky Sports in Italy and shown in several other countries. It even appeared on the giant screens in New York’s Times Square, where the club’s owners, the Cipriani family, have built much of their international reputation through Harry’s Bar.

The town’s mayor, Alessandro Barattoni, who, as always, was watching the game from the stands, said: “A champion like Ronaldinho, a world football icon, brings great visibility and today is an opportunity for us to showcase Ravenna around the world, from our stadium. It is something new for us and together with the club the municipality will try to understand how this can have a positive impact on the town.”

The local community had been excited at the prospect of Ronaldinho representing the club, but there was some regret, too. “It would have been nice if he had come to take a stroll around the city, among the people who live here and own the shops,” the barista Barbara said before the game.

So how did he end up here? The Brazilian is a friend of Ignazio Cipriani, the owner of the Giallorossi. Lorenzo Tonetti and Ariedo Braida, old acquaintances from Ronaldinho’s time at Milan, are also part of the club. They convinced him to become an investor in the club and to pull on his boots again. In addition, Ravenna are now wearing his R10 sportswear line and one of the stands bears the same name.

Ravenna are aiming high. Cipriani has never hidden the fact he is aiming for Serie A, which is ambitious for a city with a population of 156,000. And Sunday brought hope, Dinho stepping on to the pitch in a gold-trimmed kit picked by the club to celebrate his arrival (and available for sale at €120). His hair was kept in check by a black headband and he was wearing gloves on a chilly afternoon. On his back, the No 10, something more than just a number for him, the man who became a global hero thanks to his extraordinary skill and contagious smile.

A younger generation has been able to discover Ronaldinho’s genius through the endless supply of online videos showcasing his greatest moments. Children who have never seen him play know his tricks and signature moves, while their parents can relive an era of football they may feel no longer exists.

“Dad, was he strong?” a young girl asked her father as they walked hand in hand towards the stadium. “Yes, he was strong. Actually, he is strong,” he corrected himself.

Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in

One family had left Rome at 5am and travelled the 350km north just because their son had watched Ronaldinho on YouTube and wanted to see him live. Others had travelled even further, with supporters arriving from Turkey and Canada.

Ronaldinho hahas scored 299 professional goals, but his landmark 300th on his return was not to be. However, in front of a record attendance of 6,743 the way he initiated the move for Giulio Donati’s goal was ample reward for those who had turned up. Donati made his Serie A debut on 29 August 2010 for Lecce, at San Siro, against Milan, marking the Brazilian that day.

As Ronaldinho walked off at half-time, he was surrounded by a media scrum. After the game, he spoke of his desire to play again. “It all went by too quickly,” he said. “Football is like that, it’s always been like that for me.”

Who knows, perhaps he enjoyed himself so much that he wants to extend his career even further. “I don’t know, but if the president calls me, I’ll come back. It’s always a pleasure to play, I told him: ‘when he needs me, I’m there’.”

Mandorlini was effusive too. “We’re here and we’re truly proud to have been the architects of this match you played in,” he told the Brazilian. “So, if you want to play another one, that’s fine.”

Who knows what the future holds? For now, Ravenna fans will always have this: a day when a true legend connected people from around the world and allowed them, for one afternoon, to dream.

#875. We Predict Ballet Makeup Will Be the Viral Trend This Holiday Season

While ballet flats and sneakers are having their moment, beauty brands are bringing the Nutcracker and Swan Lake mood to makeup.

This holiday season, it's all about ballet-inspired makeup. Think Nutcracker and Swan Lake, but make it beauty. So many brands have been launching their limited-edition holiday collections recently with products inspired by ballet and all its iconic motifs.

We're talking everything from Ariana Grande's r.e.m. Beauty and its en pointe collection to C-Beauty brand Flower Knows and its new snow ballet line. These products don't just use a ballet aesthetic, though. The looks depicted are ones we associate with the performance. They're full of soft shimmers, flushed cheeks, delicate blue eyeshadows and glass-like skin.

We don't think we're reaching here by predicting this will become a trend during the holiday season. This makeup look will probably last throughout the rest of winter, too. Ballet flats and sneakers are already trending; so why not extend it to beauty?

It'll make it the perfect gift for the makeup-obsessed friend in your life, too! So, whether you're shopping for them or for yourself, keep scrolling to shop our favorite products to recreate this ballet-inspired trend.

Ballet is all about how the body moves, so why not make it as beautiful as possible? This affordable (and glowy) body balm highlighter gives a glassy sheen and a pearlescent finish to the collarbone, shoulders, and other high points of your body.

Featuring ballet-blue packaging and a silver pointe shoe charm, this lip mask from r.e.m. beauty's new holiday collection is incredibly dreamy. It's infused with lactic acid, tripeptide, and shea butter to leave your lips soft, glossy, and smelling deliciously gourmand.

Prefer something a little softer and blurred? This viral lip stain in the shade Romance is a cool-toned rose color that's perfect for the stage and lasts through the entire performance.

When it comes to the skin, keep it light and fresh. Cushion foundations are a perfect option for ballet makeup since they look like your real skin. While there are so many to choose from, my favorite is YSL's Soft Glow Cushion Foundation—which has a weightless, hydrated feel with medium coverage.

Highlighter is key for this look. This adorable heart-shaped one from Kimchi Chic Beauty leaves your cheekbones with a pinkish, pearlescent glow that has us absolutely obsessed.

You can't go wrong with any product from Flower Knows! The C-Beauty brand is known for its gorgeously intricate packaging, and its latest Snow Ballet collection is no exception. This blush (specifically in the shade Chiffon Ballet) glides on your cheeks, giving you a silky flush fit for a ballerina.

When it comes to eyes, opt for a sheer wash of color with some shimmer on the lid and the inner corner. This K-Beauty brand offers an eyeshadow palette with 18 shimmering and velvety soft shades.

Dior is the best designer beauty brand to choose if you're trying to recreate the ballet-inspired makeup trend. Infused with cherry oil, the Lip Glow Oil is iconic for its mirror-like, glossy shine, plumping effect,  and variety of pH-changing shades. In our opinion, though, the clear sparkly shade Cupcake is perfection.

Want a cheek palette that gives you options? This one offers blushes and highlighters in a blendable cream and powder textures that leave your cheeks soft, flushed, and naturally radiant.

Talk about a throwback! This shadow palette from Physicians Formula is arguably the first ballet-inspired makeup product, with its soft nude shades and lace packaging with a pink bow to finish it off.

#873. Why malnutrition can go unnoticed, and what that means for our health

More than 2 billion people worldwide suffer from nutrient deficiencies, most of them in the Global South. The health consequences can be devastating.

Some 50,000 deaths can be attributed to malnutrition in Germany each year, according to the German Society for Nutritional Medicine (DGEM).

The problem is that malnutrition often doesn't become apparent until the consequences are already severe.

"In most cases, you don't notice anything at first," said Matthias Pirlich, a nutritional expert and internal medicine specialist, who once served as DGEM vice president. "You could have a severe vitamin D deficiency for months before any symptoms appear at all. The same applies for vitamin B12. By the time symptoms appear, such as nerve damage, it's already too late."

A long-term B12 deficiency can damage the spinal cord, leading to numbness in the limbs, muscle weakness or even paralysis. Less common deficiency-related brain damage can cause memory loss and mental health issues.

All B vitamins play an important role in metabolism, blood formation and healthy nerve function.

Vitamins, along with various minerals such as calcium, magnesium, iron, iodine and zinc, are classed as micronutrients. The body needs to source them from food, as it cannot produce them itself. Our bodies also need macronutrients like carbohydrates, carbohydrates, protein and fats that provide us with energy.

If the body consumes less food than it needs to maintain all bodily functions over a prolonged period of time, then this is known as undernutrition. A recent World Food Organization (FAO) report estimates that approximately 645 million people worldwide suffer from chronic undernutrition.

Malnutrition, on the other hand, occurs when we consume enough calories but lack certain macronutrients or micronutrients in our food. This, too, can make one sick over time and even prove fatal. About 2 billion people worldwide suffer from this so-called hidden hunger, most of them in the Global South. That said, even some people in industrialized nations lack important micronutrients in their nutrition.

One study, for instance, found that just under three-quarters of the US population did not meet the recommended daily intake of vitamin D between 2007 and 2010, with more than two-thirds falling short of the recommended amount of vitamin E. And in Germany, about one-third of the population suffered from vitamin D deficiency in 2017, according to the German Nutrition Society. Such deficiency can cause bone, joint and muscle pain. It may also lead to an increased risk of falls and bone fractures.

About one-third of Germans also had an insufficient intake of iodine, a trace element that is indispensable for the production of thyroid hormones. Iodine deficiency can therefore disrupt normal thyroid function. Not only that — during pregnancy, a baby's brain and nervous system can only properly develop with an adequate supply of iodine.

The cultivation of agricultural produce with partially long shelf life or high yields has in some cases caused a decrease in the micronutrient content of fruits, vegetables and grains. Whether this drop in micronutrients is impacting human health, however, is a matter of debate.

Malnutrition can result from an unbalanced diet that, while filling and providing energy, lacks essential micronutrients. Examples of such empty calories include fast food and highly processed foods, as well as white bread and white rice.

Poverty is often the reason for such an unbalanced diet, for example when people in the Global South can only afford to buy staples such as flour or rice.

Another study found that in Germany, households at risk of poverty are more likely to consume foods that are low in nutrients and high in calories.

Depression is also associated with an increased risk of nutrient deficiency. "People often lose their appetite, and when they neglect their self-care, they may end up eating a very unbalanced diet," Pirlich told DW. His research shows that older adults and people who live alone often develop malnutrition, too. The risk also increases the more medications a person takes.

Many diseases result in the body being less efficient at absorbing or utilizing nutrients through the intestines. This applies to people with inflammatory or chronic disease, such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, liver disease and cancer.

The DGEM estimates that some 30% of all patients receiving inpatient care in Germany are affected by or at risk of malnutrition. Yet health insurance data shows that only about 1% of patients are screened and treated for nutrient deficiencies.

Often, patients' malnutrition worsens during their hospital stay. The consequences can be serious, potentially causing additional complications, delayed recuperation, longer hospital stays and even increased mortality rates. This results in higher healthcare expenditure, amounting to billions each year.

German policymakers and medical associations are therefore developing a plan to better screen for and treat malnutrition in hospitals. The road map will be ready by 2027 and copy the Dutch approach in the sense that all patients are checked for nutritional deficiencies upon hospital admission.

Pirlich wants to see such screenings for at-risk groups in outpatient clinics, too: "This includes all those with chronic and serious illnesses and, above all, older adults."

To prevent poverty-related malnutrition, Pirlich suggests increased access to healthy food, offering free school meals as an example.

The nutritional expert recommends eating a diet that is varied and largely plant-based. "Secondary plant compounds have a very positive effect, and if you eat a highly diverse diet, you consume many different foods that are [nutritionally] beneficial," said Pirlich.

There's a simple rule of thumb: The more colorful your food, the better.

Also, cook vegetables as gently as possible, because overheating and keeping them warm for too long destroys their vitamins. Long storage periods also lead to vitamin loss, so it makes sense to go for seasonal and regional foods in particular.

But even when ensuring a healthy and balanced diet, some people still develop a nutrient deficiency. A blood test can provide clarity, and dietary supplements may help make up for the deficiency.

This article was originally written in German.

#872. Azeez to Andrés: seven smart-looking Premier League deadline day deals

An 18-year-old who has played at two major international tournaments and the division’s top clearance maker from last season also feature

A tricky, exciting, quick and versatile midfielder, Azeez has proven himself in the Championship with Millwall over the past two seasons and now deserves a chance to test himself in the top flight.

Brighton had been chasing him for a while and struck a deal on deadline day for a very reasonable reported initial £12.5m, rising to £15m. If he can make the step up and produce anything like his second-tier form, he’ll be a steal.

He is a high-volume producer at the sharp end of the pitch, constantly making things happen that threaten the opposition’s goal, but standing out most for his crossing. He ranked top of the Championship last season for open-play crosses (227) and expected assists from crosses (6.71 xA).

He also ranked fourth for dribble attempts (131), ninth for shots (95), sixth for chances created from open play (58). He created good-quality chances, too; only two players created more big chances than he did (18), and he ranked fourth for expected assists. His 9.12 xA alongside only seven assists suggests he may benefit from playing alongside better finishers.

A hugely exciting prospect. Despite being 18, Mbaye has significant and noteworthy experience under his belt. Last year he made six appearances, including in the final, for Senegal at the Africa Cup of Nations and this summer he made four appearances at the World Cup. He has also played in two Ligue 1 title-winning campaigns, including 2024-25, when he became the youngest player in PSG’s history to start a game, and won the Champions League in both of those seasons

He is a dribbling and ball-carrying menace, who always looks as if he’s about to do something special. Among players to play at least 900 minutes in Ligue 1 last season, he was 11th for carries (moving at least five metres with the ball) per 90, with 20.0, and 12th for progressive carries (moving at least five metres upfield with the ball) per 90, with 10.3. Most of the players above him in both lists are defenders, who naturally have more space to move into.

He was third for take-on-ending carries, or running with the ball for at least five metres before attempting to beat an opponent with a dribble, with 2.9 per 90. And he also has end product to boot. He scored at Afcon and the World Cup despite limited minutes and his 0.45 goals or assists per 90 for PSG last season is not to be sniffed at.

Danso had a pretty impossible task over his two years at Tottenham. He was the back-up to the first-choice centre-backs Cristian Romero and Micky van de Ven, playing intermittently on both sides of central defence in dysfunctional teams jumping between styles of play, and he very rarely played for any consistent run of games.

He was unfairly compared with the players he was replacing for much of his time there, but the truth is he was always reliable enough. He excelled, however, when Romero got injured during the run-in last season and he was called upon in Spurs’ time of need as they scraped clear of relegation.

He may not be the best on the ball – though he is hardly terrible – but he is an excellent deep defender. Among those to play at least 1,000 minutes in the Premier League last season, Danso ranked first for clearances (8.2 per 90) and headed clearances (6.3), and was fifth for aerial duels won (4.8 per 90).

He could thrive at Sunderland, who spent more of their out-of-possession game time in a low block than any other team in the Premier League last season (25%). Danso could be perfectly at home in this setup, paired alongside the player he beat into second place for clearances and headed clearances: Dan Ballard.

It was always said during Pep Guardiola’s time at Manchester City that attackers had their wings clipped in terms of individual freedom, limited to playing within the parameters of the manager’s meticulous gameplan.

But dribbling ability became increasingly important in the final years of his reign, with Jérémy Doku and Antoine Semenyo on the wings and Rayan Cherki in between. Doku (162) and Semenyo (144) ranked first and second for dribbles attempted in the Premier League last season, with Cherki ninth (111). They also ranked first (84), fourth (59) and eighth (51), respectively, for dribbles completed.

With the deadline-day addition of Ndiaye, City have gone in even harder on dribbling ability under Enzo Maresca. The Senegal international ranked second for dribbles attempted (136) and dribbles completed (73) in the Premier League last season.

Fernandez-Pardo’s versatility is a major attraction. He’s comfortable playing off the left and cutting in on to his right foot, or as a No 9. Although not the bulkiest, he has explosive pace and promises to be a threat in behind.

The Belgium international is arguably at his most threatening when running with the ball because he does so with such purpose. His 122 carries progressing the ball at least 10 metres upfield in Ligue 1 last term were bettered by only seven players, several of whom were defenders.

On top of that, he ranked top for carries into the penalty area (69) and seventh for carries ending with a shot or chance created (39).

Fofana appeared to be enjoying a swift rise in 2024-25, only for a serious ankle injury to massively disrupt his development in 2025-26. Sunderland will be hoping they can get him back to the levels shown the season before last, when he was a real livewire on Lyon’s left flank.

He contributed nine goal involvements (five goals, four assists) in 1,586 minutes in Ligue 1 in 2024-25, averaging one every 176 minutes. Only eight forwards (900+ mins) averaged more expected assists per 90 (0.25).

The most eye-catching aspects of his game, however, were his dynamism and pace. He could be difficult to stop once moving, and this made him a very useful outlet. Among Ligue 1 forwards (900+ mins), his 16.6 carries per 90 ranked him sixth, and he moved up to third for progressive carries per 90 (11.5).

Fofana is direct, exciting and has significant potential. He is a player Sunderland could make a profit on if he reaches the levels previously expected.

Andrés arrived to bolster Brighton’s midfield options after Carlos Baleba’s exit to Manchester United. Although a different type of midfielder to the Cameroonian, Chema is another with vast potential.

A product of Real Madrid’s academy, Chema joined Stuttgart last summer. During his sole campaign in the Bundesliga, he was in and out of the team but caught the eye at the base of their midfield.

Comparisons have been made to Rodri because of his physical attributes and nominal role as a holding midfielder. He doesn’t have anything like the same influence in possession but Chema is tidy on the ball.

It’s what he offers defensively that is most notable, however. He’s been broadly praised for his anticipation and reading of the game, ranking second among midfielders (900+ mins) since the start of last season for interceptions per 90 in the Bundesliga (2.3).
